title: AGI Rideout: Managing Risk on the Road to Advanced AI
gist: In a RAND podcast, David Frelinger and Karl Mueller argue that the US should stop framing the race to AGI with China as winner-takes-all. They propose an 'AGI Rideout' strategy, borrowed from nuclear survivability, that hedges against conflict during a long and uneven transition. It would rest on new AI-focused intelligence and defense organizations, signaling, and selective cooperation with China. They see the main war risks as AI super-weapons, preventive war by a side that is losing, and AI-enabled regional aggression such as a move on Taiwan.

insights.claim: Treating AI competition as a winner-takes-all race, in which one state dominates via an intelligence explosion after crossing an AGI threshold, has bad consequences because it neglects stabilizing the race along the way.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Challenges the dominant 'race to AGI' framing that drives policy and capex narratives.

insights.claim: Because the AGI race runs on expectations about the future, self-induced fears and mutual misperception between the US and China create an unstable dynamic during the transition.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Perception-driven instability raises geopolitical tail risk around AI milestones.
insights.locator: Yeah, it also creates a situation

insights.claim: Being the most advanced AGI state does not make a country invulnerable to what a less advanced rival can do with AI to impede, injure or threaten it, so winning the race does not guarantee safety.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that AI leadership alone secures strategic dominance.
insights.quote: being the most advanced state in the AGI race doesn't make you invulnerable to the things that your less advanced rival might be able to do with AI

insights.claim: Game designers observe that players do 'crazy things' when they can see the end of the game; treating AI as an open-ended problem rather than a finish line changes behavior toward stability.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A finish-line framing encourages reckless, all-in moves by states and firms.
insights.quote: If you have an open-ended game, everything changes.
insights.locator: Yeah, and oddly, looking at other

themes.theme: Shooting the rapids: limited control, long transition

insights.claim: The propulsive force behind AI progress comes mainly from profit-seeking private firms, and the government has only limited ability to influence its speed or direction.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Policy is unlikely to slow the private AI buildout; the state reacts rather than steers.
insights.quote: The propulsive force for AI progress mostly comes from the private sector, as the AI firms are pursuing profit
insights.locator: To a significant extent, we don't see

insights.claim: The AGI transition is likely to last much longer than many imagine, because AI develops unevenly across domains and is hard to diffuse into economies and societies.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Argues against fast-takeoff timelines for economic impact, implying slower diffusion.
insights.quote: given the difficulties of diffusing it into economies and in the society, some of this will extend considerably longer than some advocates imagine.
insights.locator: Yeah, and I think the open-ended

insights.claim: The authors liken the AI race to 'shooting the rapids' on an unmapped river rather than a regatta: survival matters, and the path is not under any one actor's control.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A framing that favors resilience and hedging over maximal speed.
insights.locator: We use the "shooting the rapids" metaphor

insights.claim: 'Rideout' is borrowed from nuclear strategy. The aim is a transition like the one from 1950s fears of a surprise first strike to the late-1960s survivable arsenals, which gave both superpowers more options and made crises less intense.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Suggests AI stability depends on survivability and resilience, not on first-mover advantage.

insights.claim: Robustness makes the system forgiving of errors and removes the urgency for all-or-nothing action; in uncertain, high-risk settings, time is an asset.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Resilience investments reduce pressure for escalation.
insights.quote: you want to turn the temperature down, you want to get time—time is an asset.

insights.claim: Pathway one to an AI-related war is an adversary using AI to develop a capability, such as a biological wonder weapon, to inflict vast harm on the US.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Bio-AI risk is a recognized national-security vector that is driving policy.
insights.locator: The way we break it down

insights.claim: Pathway two is a preventive war launched by a state that is losing the AI race and fears that a US victory would mean US domination of the world.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Pulling far ahead in AI could itself raise the risk of conflict, a non-obvious second-order effect.

insights.claim: Pathway three is AI-enabled capabilities persuading Beijing it could attack Taiwan cheaply and successfully, starting a war the US joins that then escalates, a risk that does not require anyone to reach AGI first.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Pre-AGI military AI could destabilize the Taiwan Strait, the key node for semiconductors.
insights.quote: China developing AI-enabled capabilities that could make leaders in Beijing think they could inexpensively and successfully attack Taiwan.

insights.claim: Even a limited war over Taiwan could wipe out chips vital to current LLM approaches and hyperscale server farms, so hedging against conflict protects the AI buildout itself.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Direct link between Taiwan conflict risk and the AI compute supply chain.
insights.quote: even a limited war over Taiwan, could lead to loss of a lot of resources that are necessary like chips that are vital for our current approaches using LLMs and hyperscale server farms.

insights.claim: The authors recommend two new organizations: an AI-focused intelligence body issuing targeted warnings about adversary AI, and a defense body that turns those warnings into rapid-development programs.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Points to likely new defense and intelligence spending on AI monitoring and rapid acquisition.
insights.locator: And that part is actually critical

insights.claim: Hedging spending largely complements the pursuit of AI leadership, but in a resource-constrained world it takes the marginal dollar away from other programs of record, even within a trillion-dollar budget.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Expect budget reallocation toward AI hedging within defense spending.
insights.quote: Even inside a large trillion dollar sort of budget, you can make some trade-offs

insights.claim: Delaying hedging leads to worse, less effective crash programs later, while continuous effort builds knowledge and signals intentions to adversaries.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Early, steady procurement beats reactive crash spending.
insights.quote: you wait until too late, you have a crash program that's even worse

insights.claim: The most important near-term action is to put money behind the strategy and openly signal it, to adversaries, the rest of government and the public, to position the US as the 'responsible party'.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Watch for funded AI-stability initiatives as a policy signal.
insights.quote: one of the main things it can do is it puts money against it.

insights.claim: A well-executed Rideout strategy would look uneventful, even invisible: major conflict avoided, deterrence intact, and surprises contained.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Success is measured by the absence of events, which makes it hard to observe or price.
insights.quote: a well-executed Rideout strategy should be almost invisible

insights.claim: China may already follow a rideout-like strategy, staying close to the US and excelling in niches rather than leaping ahead; China-expert players in RAND's AI-competition wargames often describe this approach.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Suggests China's AI posture is a fast-follower strategy rather than a sprint, with implications for its compute and model strategy.
insights.quote: the goal was not to leap into the forefront of the competition right away but rather to stay close to the United States and stay in the game

insights.claim: Playing down the winner-take-all framing could open US-China cooperation on AI safety standards and beneficial uses such as public health.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A path, though uncertain, toward AI standards cooperation that could ease some tech-war tail risk.
insights.locator: I think one would be the potential

insights.claim: This is a geopolitical competition with a large technology component, not a purely technological one, so cooperation will be hard even where interests align.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations of a US-China AI détente.
insights.quote: This is not a technological competition, it's a geopolitical competition with a big technological component to it.

insights.claim: Non-geopolitical AI risks, including economic disruption, societal change and autonomous agents 'getting loose', may be even more dire than the worst-case geopolitical scenarios, and they call for the same anticipate-and-adapt approach.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Flags economic disruption and agent risk as under-hedged.
insights.quote: some of those threats may be even more dire than the sort of worst-case scenarios that we're thinking about in the context of the geopolitical competition.
